      A simplified experiment: rates stay constant, interest compounds once a year, and no money is added or withdrawn. Taxes and fees are excluded. The lunch follows average inflation; real prices vary. These are examples, not current rates or forecasts.

      01

      Inflation

      Inflation is a general rise in the prices of goods and services across the economy over time. When prices rise, the same amount of money buys less.

      At 3% inflation, a $100 basket costs $103 after one year.
      02

      Purchasing power

      Purchasing power means what your money can buy. If your money grows more slowly than prices, your purchasing power falls—even if your account balance goes up.

      More money in your account doesn't always mean you can afford more.
      03

      Interest

      Interest is money you earn on savings, or pay for borrowing. With compound interest, your savings earn interest on both the original money and earlier interest.

      To gain buying power in this model, your savings rate must beat inflation.
      HOW THEY CONNECT

      Why do interest rates matter for inflation?

      Central banks can raise policy interest rates to make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive. This can slow spending and help reduce inflation over time. The savings rate above is what your account earns; changing it here doesn't automatically change inflation.

      See the simple math

      Future balance = starting savings × (1 + interest rate)years

      Buying power in today's dollars = future balance ÷ (1 + inflation rate)years

      Future lunch price = $10 × (1 + inflation rate)years

      Use rates as decimals: 3% = 0.03. If interest equals inflation, buying power stays the same. Lower positive inflation means prices rise more slowly, not that prices fall.

      Key terms for this model

      Open a term for a definition and a quick example.

      Back to activity
      Inflation rate

      The percentage change in the overall price level over a stated period. The simulator uses an annual rate.

      If a price index rises from 120 to 126 in one year, the inflation rate is 5%, not 6%.

      (New index − old index) ÷ old index × 100

      The index measures the price level; the inflation rate measures how quickly it changes.

      Market basket

      A collection of goods and services used to track prices. In a simple fixed-basket example, compare the cost of the same items and quantities over time.

      Our example basket starts with $50 of groceries, $30 of transport, and $20 of supplies: $100 altogether.

      Using several items shows a broader picture than the price of one lunch.

      Price index

      An index compares a value with a reference point. A price index compares price levels over time, often setting the base period to 100.

      If the same basket costs $100 in the base period and $110 later, its index is 110: prices are 10% above the base period.

      Current basket cost ÷ base-period cost × 100

      This is our simplified fixed-basket formula. An index of 110 does not tell you how quickly prices changed in the last year.

      Consumer Price Index (CPI)

      Consumer prices are the prices households pay. In the U.S., the CPI tracks average price changes for a representative basket bought by urban consumers.

      Housing, food, transport, and other purchases contribute to the index. Categories with larger spending shares carry more weight.

      CPI is a real-world price index. Our small basket only illustrates the idea; it does not calculate the official CPI.

      Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics
      Deflation

      A sustained decline in the general price level: the inflation rate is negative. A dollar can buy more as prices fall, if your money stays the same.

      At −2% over one year, a $100 basket becomes $98 and its price index becomes 98. Try the Deflation preset in Explore.

      Inflation slowing from 5% to 2% is disinflation: prices still rise. A sale on one product is not economy-wide deflation. Falling prices can also come with falling incomes and make debts harder to repay.

      Source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
